stem: A 64-year-old woman has episodes of flushing of the face and watery diarrhea for eight months, and now has wheezing with these spells. A new murmur is heard at the left lower sternal border, loudest in inspiration. Imaging shows several hepatic lesions and a small mass in the terminal ileum.
oneliner: 64F + flushing, diarrhea, wheeze + tricuspid murmur + liver lesions + ileal mass → which urine test?
ask: Which urine test result is most likely?

whyNot.B: **VMA** rises with pheochromocytoma or neuroblastoma, which cause hypertension and sweating rather than diarrhea and valve disease
whyNot.C: **Metanephrines** also point to pheochromocytoma, with paroxysmal hypertension and headache
whyNot.D: **Free cortisol** is elevated in Cushing syndrome, with central obesity and striae
whyNot.E: **HVA** is raised in neuroblastoma, a childhood tumor

why: A midgut carcinoid with **liver metastases** releases **serotonin** past the liver's metabolism, causing **flushing, diarrhea, wheeze** and **right-sided valve fibrosis**. Serotonin is broken down to **5-HIAA**, which is raised in the urine.

idea.rule: Carcinoid syndrome = serotonin excess = urinary 5-HIAA up.
also: Liver metastases are needed for syndrome from a gut tumor
Right-sided plaques: tricuspid regurgitation and pulmonic stenosis
Niacin deficiency (pellagra) can develop
Octreotide controls symptoms

stem: A 5-week-old first-born boy has vomited forcefully after almost every feed for 10 days. The vomit is milky and free of bile, and he is hungry again straight after. He is mildly dehydrated, and rolling waves can be seen crossing his upper abdomen after a feed. Blood gas shows a raised pH and bicarbonate.
oneliner: 5-week-old M + first-born + projectile nonbilious vomiting + visible waves + alkalosis → which imaging finding?
ask: Which imaging finding is most likely?

options.A: A thickened, elongated pyloric muscle with a target-like cross-section
options.B: Double-bubble sign with no gas beyond the duodenum
options.C: Corkscrew-shaped duodenum on a contrast study
options.D: Target-shaped mass in the right lower quadrant
options.E: Dilated small bowel loops with soap-bubble gas pattern

whyNot.B: Duodenal atresia usually presents on **day one** with vomiting that is typically **bilious**; this infant is 5 weeks old with non-bilious vomit
whyNot.C: A corkscrew duodenum marks **malrotation with volvulus**, which causes **bilious** vomiting
whyNot.D: An ileocolic intussusception produces a mass with **colicky pain and red-currant stool**, not feed-related vomiting with alkalosis
whyNot.E: Soap-bubble meconium-type gas is **neonatal ileus** from the first days of life; this baby vomits only after feeds at 5 weeks

why: Hypertrophy of the pyloric muscle narrows the gastric outlet. Ultrasound shows a **pyloric muscle thickness over about 3-4 mm** and a **channel longer than about 15-17 mm**, appearing as a **target** in cross-section. Vomiting loses gastric HCl, causing **hypochloremic hypokalemic metabolic alkalosis**.

idea.rule: Nonbilious projectile vomiting at 3-6 weeks with an obstructed gastric outlet means pyloric muscle hypertrophy, confirmed by ultrasound.
also: Palpable olive-shaped epigastric mass
Gastric outlet obstruction loses HCl: hypochloremic metabolic alkalosis
Bilious vomiting points to obstruction beyond the ampulla (atresia, malrotation)
Associated with macrolide exposure in early infancy

stem: A 4-year-old boy attends day care, where several other children have been ill. For 3 days he has had fever, crampy lower abdominal pain, repeated small stools with mucus and blood, and a constant urge to pass stool. A stool smear is stained and examined under the microscope.
oneliner: 4M + day-care outbreak + fever + tenesmus + bloody mucoid stools → which stool microscopy result?
ask: Which stool smear result is most likely?

options.A: Oocysts staining on modified acid-fast preparation
options.B: Numerous neutrophils on methylene blue stain
options.C: Flagellated trophozoites with a sucking disc
options.E: No leukocytes seen on methylene blue stain

whyNot.A: Cryptosporidium gives **watery, non-bloody** diarrhea; this child passes **blood and mucus**
whyNot.C: Giardia gives **greasy, non-bloody** diarrhea with bloating; this child has **tenesmus and blood**
whyNot.D: Eosinophils and Charcot-Leyden crystals suggest a **helminth or allergic** process, not **fever with bloody mucoid stools**
whyNot.E: A smear without leukocytes fits toxin or viral watery diarrhea; his **fever, tenesmus and bloody mucoid stools** show mucosal invasion

why: Invasive organisms (**Shigella**, Campylobacter, Salmonella, EIEC, Entamoeba) injure the colonic mucosa and bring in **neutrophils**, seen as **fecal leukocytes** on methylene blue, with blood and mucus. **Toxin-mediated or viral** diarrhea (ETEC, norovirus, rotavirus) leaves the stool smear **without leukocytes**.

idea.rule: Fever, tenesmus and blood in stool = invasive colitis = fecal leukocytes; watery diarrhea without blood = toxin or virus = none.
also: Shigella: tiny infectious dose, spreads in day care
Traveler diarrhea from ETEC: watery stool, no leukocytes
Norovirus and rotavirus: no fecal leukocytes
Fecal lactoferrin and calprotectin also mark neutrophilic inflammation

stem: A 9-year-old boy has had recurrent bloating, loud bowel sounds and watery, non-bloody diarrhea for 3 months, always within hours of milk or ice cream. The symptoms stop when dairy is removed from his diet. His growth is normal. A stool sample and a breath test are done after a dairy load.
oneliner: 9M + bloating + borborygmi + watery nonbloody diarrhea + settles off dairy → which stool and breath results?
ask: Which set of stool and breath test results is most likely?

options.A: Low fecal elastase with normal stool pH
options.C: Alkaline stool pH with a negative hydrogen breath test
options.D: Acidic stool with reducing substances and raised breath hydrogen
options.E: High fecal fat with low fecal elastase

whyNot.A: Low elastase marks **pancreatic insufficiency** with greasy stools and poor growth; his stools are **watery** and his growth is **normal**
whyNot.B: Leukocytes and blood come with **invasive infection**; he has **no fever or bloody stool**
whyNot.C: A negative breath test would argue against a carbohydrate problem, but his symptoms **follow dairy and resolve without it**
whyNot.E: High fecal fat means **steatorrhea** from fat malabsorption; his stools are **watery** and tied to **dairy sugar**

answer: Acidic stool with reducing substances and a raised breath hydrogen
why: Unabsorbed lactose reaches the colon, where bacteria **ferment it to short-chain fatty acids and hydrogen**. Stools become **acidic (pH under 5.5) and test positive for reducing substances**, the unabsorbed sugar draws water osmotically, and exhaled **hydrogen rises**.

idea.rule: Carbohydrate malabsorption = osmotic watery diarrhea, acidic stool, reducing substances, and breath hydrogen.
also: Lactase deficiency is the commonest cause, with a normal intestinal biopsy
Secondary lactase loss follows viral gastroenteritis and celiac disease
Sucrase-isomaltase deficiency gives the same findings after sucrose
Glucose-galactose malabsorption (SGLT1 defect) gives acidic stool with reducing substances

stem: A 45-year-old man has diabetes mellitus, bronze-tinted skin and tender, firm hepatomegaly. He has recently developed heart failure with a dilated, poorly contracting left ventricle, and two relatives died of heart disease in their forties. A liver biopsy is taken.
oneliner: 45M + diabetes + bronze skin + hepatomegaly + dilated cardiomyopathy + young relatives died of heart disease → which liver biopsy stain result?
ask: Which liver biopsy finding is most likely?

options.A: Apple-green birefringence under polarized light after Congo red
options.B: Hepatocyte pigment staining blue with Prussian blue

whyNot.A: Amyloid causes restrictive, not **dilated**, cardiomyopathy and does not explain **bronze skin with diabetes**
whyNot.C: Copper overload gives liver and **neuropsychiatric** disease in the young; his picture is **diabetes, bronze skin and dilated heart**
whyNot.D: Alpha-1 antitrypsin globules cause **emphysema and liver disease**; nothing in the stem suggests lung disease
whyNot.E: Glycogen storage disease presents with **enzyme-deficiency** pictures in infancy or childhood, not **bronze skin and diabetes** in a middle-aged man

answer: Parenchymal iron (hemosiderin) staining blue with Prussian blue
why: Excess iron deposits as **hemosiderin** in hepatocytes, pancreatic islets, myocardium, skin and joints. **Prussian blue** turns the iron **blue** and shows it in the **parenchymal** cells; this explains cirrhosis, **diabetes, bronze skin and dilated cardiomyopathy**.

idea.rule: Hemochromatosis = iron in parenchymal cells (Prussian blue), damaging liver, pancreas, heart, skin and joints.
also: HFE C282Y homozygosity is the usual genetic cause
Iron studies: high transferrin saturation and ferritin
Treatment is phlebotomy; increased risk of hepatocellular carcinoma
Hemosiderosis from transfusion deposits iron in macrophages first

stem: A 44-year-old man who has drunk heavily for 25 years comes in with abdominal swelling. He is jaundiced, has shifting dullness on percussion and a firm, nodular liver edge. His platelet count is low.
oneliner: 44M + 25 years heavy alcohol + jaundice + ascites + nodular liver + low platelets → which additional physical finding?
ask: Which additional physical finding is most likely?

options.A: Kayser-Fleischer rings at the corneal edge
options.B: Bronze skin with arthropathy of the second and third MCP joints
options.E: Spider angiomas on the chest with palmar erythema

whyNot.A: Corneal copper rings accompany **Wilson disease** in the young; his cause of liver damage is **long alcohol use**
whyNot.B: Bronze skin with MCP arthropathy marks **iron overload**; nothing here points to it and alcohol explains his **cirrhosis**
whyNot.C: Xanthelasma accompanies **cholestatic disease** such as primary biliary cholangitis, whereas he has **alcohol-related** disease
whyNot.D: Erythema nodosum arises with **sarcoidosis, IBD or infection**, none of which are suggested

why: A cirrhotic liver **clears estrogen poorly**, and more androgen is converted to estrogen (aromatization). The resulting **hyperestrogenism** produces **spider angiomas**, **palmar erythema**, **gynecomastia** and testicular atrophy in men.

idea.rule: Cirrhosis causes hyperestrogenism: spider angiomas, palmar erythema, gynecomastia, testicular atrophy.
also: Gynecomastia and testicular atrophy in men with cirrhosis
Loss of male-pattern body hair from the same estrogen-androgen imbalance
Pregnancy, another high-estrogen state, also brings spider angiomas and palmar erythema
Cirrhosis from any cause, not only alcohol, gives these signs

stem: A 40-year-old man has 3 weeks of malaise, nausea and right upper quadrant pain, followed by dark urine. He began a new sexual relationship 2 months ago and has never been vaccinated against hepatitis B. Screening at a blood donation 4 months ago was negative. Total bilirubin is 4 mg/dL, ALT 1,700 U/L and AST 1,500 U/L, and HBV DNA is 2 × 10⁸ IU/mL.
oneliner: 40M + 3 weeks malaise, RUQ pain, dark urine + new partner + negative screen 4 months ago + ALT 1,700 + HBV DNA 2 × 10⁸ → which serology?
ask: Which hepatitis B serology pattern is most likely?

whyNot.B: Chronic infection means **HBsAg for over 6 months** with IgG anti-HBc; his **screen was negative 4 months ago**
whyNot.C: The window period comes **after HBsAg clears**; with a viral load of **2 × 10⁸** the surface antigen is still circulating
whyNot.D: Resolved infection is **past and silent**; he is acutely ill with **high DNA**
whyNot.E: Vaccine immunity gives anti-HBs alone; he was **never vaccinated** and has **active hepatitis**

answer: HBsAg +, HBeAg +, IgM anti-HBc +, anti-HBs − (acute, highly infectious)
why: Acute hepatitis B with active replication shows **HBsAg** and **HBeAg** (high infectivity) and **IgM anti-HBc**, the marker of recent infection. **Anti-HBs** has not yet formed. Aminotransferases in the thousands reflect **CD8⁺ T-cell injury** of infected hepatocytes.

idea.rule: IgM anti-HBc marks recent infection; HBsAg beyond 6 months with IgG anti-HBc marks chronic infection.
also: Window period: HBsAg gone, anti-HBs not yet present, IgM anti-HBc the only marker
Resolved infection: IgG anti-HBc plus anti-HBs, HBsAg negative
HBeAg with high HBV DNA marks high infectivity
Vaccination gives anti-HBs only, with no anti-HBc

stem: A 25-year-old man who moved from Pakistan two months ago has fatigue. He drinks no alcohol, takes no medications and has no muscle pain. He is not jaundiced and his total bilirubin is 0.8 mg/dL. Hepatitis C antibody is positive and HCV RNA is detectable.
oneliner: 25M + recent immigrant from Pakistan + fatigue + no alcohol, no jaundice + HCV antibody and RNA positive → which aminotransferase pattern?
ask: Which aminotransferase pattern is most likely?

options.B: ALP and GGT raised, aminotransferases normal
options.C: ALT and AST both raised, with ALT higher than AST
options.D: AST and CK markedly raised, ALT normal
options.E: AST and ALT normal, indirect bilirubin raised

whyNot.A: This is the **alcoholic hepatitis** pattern; he drinks **no alcohol**
whyNot.B: That is **cholestasis**, which brings jaundice or itch; he has **no jaundice** and normal bilirubin
whyNot.D: That is **muscle injury**; he has **no muscle pain** and a proven liver infection
whyNot.E: That is **Gilbert or hemolysis**; his **bilirubin is normal** and he has active viral hepatitis

answer: ALT above AST, both raised (viral hepatitis)
why: Viral hepatitis injures hepatocytes diffusely, and **ALT**, a cytosolic liver enzyme, is released more than **AST**, which is also found in muscle, heart and mitochondria. The ratio is therefore **below 1**, unlike the **AST:ALT above 2** of alcoholic hepatitis.

idea.rule: Viral hepatitis gives ALT above AST; alcoholic hepatitis gives AST:ALT above 2.
also: Muscle injury raises AST and CK with a normal ALT
Cholestasis raises ALP and GGT, with aminotransferases less affected
Once viral hepatitis progresses to cirrhosis, AST can overtake ALT
Councilman bodies (apoptotic hepatocytes) are seen in viral hepatitis

stem: A 27-year-old man has mild jaundice and an enlarged liver. His alkaline phosphatase is three times the upper limit of normal. He has no bone pain or fractures and takes no medications.
oneliner: 27M + mild jaundice + hepatomegaly + ALP 3× normal + no bone symptoms → which result shows a liver source?
ask: Which additional result would best show that the alkaline phosphatase comes from the liver?

whyNot.A: High calcium suggests **bone resorption** (metastases, hyperparathyroidism), which points away from the liver
whyNot.B: Osteocalcin comes from **osteoblasts**, so it would support a **bone** source
whyNot.C: A ratio over 2 suggests **alcohol-related** injury; it says nothing about where the **ALP** comes from
whyNot.D: Hydroxyproline reflects **collagen breakdown in bone** (as in Paget disease), the opposite of the liver source

answer: Raised GGT alongside the raised ALP (hepatobiliary source)
why: ALP is made in bile canalicular membranes, bone and placenta, but **GGT** is found in **bile duct epithelium and hepatocytes** and **not in bone**. A raised GGT together with a raised ALP therefore places the source in the **hepatobiliary tree**.

idea.rule: Raised ALP with raised GGT is hepatobiliary; raised ALP with normal GGT points to bone.
also: Paget disease and bone metastases raise ALP with a normal GGT
Growing children and pregnancy raise ALP from bone or placenta
Alcohol and phenytoin can induce GGT
A cholestatic pattern combines raised ALP, GGT and conjugated bilirubin

stem: A 22-year-old woman has had 6 months of difficulty swallowing both solids and liquids from the start, with regurgitation of undigested food and 4 kg of weight loss. She has no heartburn, skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon, and no episodes of chest pain with swallowing. Esophageal manometry is performed.
oneliner: 22F + dysphagia to solids and liquids from the start + regurgitation + weight loss + no heartburn, no skin changes → which manometry pattern?
ask: Which esophageal manometry pattern is most likely?

options.A: Resting LES pressure low, relaxation complete, peristalsis normal
options.B: Resting LES pressure high, relaxation incomplete, peristalsis absent
options.C: Resting LES pressure normal, relaxation complete, simultaneous high-amplitude contractions
options.D: Resting LES pressure very low, relaxation complete, distal peristalsis absent
options.E: Resting LES pressure high, relaxation complete, peristalsis normal

whyNot.A: That is the **reflux** pattern; she has **no heartburn**
whyNot.C: That is **diffuse spasm**, which causes **intermittent chest pain** with swallowing; she has none
whyNot.D: That is **scleroderma** esophagus; she has no **skin thickening or Raynaud phenomenon**
whyNot.E: With complete relaxation and normal peristalsis, **liquids** would pass; her trouble with **both solids and liquids from the start** needs failed relaxation

answer: High resting LES pressure, incomplete relaxation, absent peristalsis (achalasia)
why: Loss of inhibitory **NO/VIP neurons** in the myenteric plexus leaves the LES unable to relax and the esophageal body without peristalsis. Manometry shows a **high resting LES pressure**, **incomplete relaxation** on swallowing and **absent peristalsis**.

idea.rule: Achalasia: loss of inhibitory neurons gives a tight LES, no relaxation and no peristalsis.
also: Chagas disease destroys the myenteric plexus and mimics achalasia
Scleroderma: low LES pressure and absent peristalsis, so reflux
Diffuse spasm: simultaneous high-amplitude contractions with normal LES relaxation
Achalasia raises the risk of esophageal squamous cell carcinoma

stem: An 18-year-old woman asks for colon cancer screening. Her father was found to have colonic polyps in his teens and died of colon cancer at 36, and her grandfather died of colon cancer at 45. She has no diarrhea, rectal bleeding or abdominal pain, and no pigmented spots on her lips. Colonoscopy is performed.
oneliner: 18F + father with teen polyps, colon cancer death at 36 + grandfather at 45 + asymptomatic, no lip pigmentation → colonoscopy finding?
ask: Which colonoscopy finding is most likely?

options.D: Hundreds of adenomas throughout colon and rectum

whyNot.A: This is **Peutz-Jeghers**, which has **mucocutaneous pigmentation**; she has none
whyNot.B: This is **Lynch syndrome**, with few adenomas; her father had **polyps already in his teens**
whyNot.C: This is **ulcerative colitis**, which causes **bloody diarrhea**; she has no symptoms
whyNot.E: This is **Crohn disease**, with **pain and diarrhea**; she has neither

answer: Hundreds of adenomatous polyps carpeting the colon (familial adenomatous polyposis)
why: FAP is an autosomal dominant **APC** mutation (5q). **Hundreds to thousands** of adenomas appear from adolescence and **always include the rectum**, so colon cancer is almost certain without **prophylactic colectomy**.

idea.rule: FAP: APC (5q) mutation, over 100 adenomas from adolescence, rectum always involved.
also: Gardner syndrome adds osteomas, soft-tissue tumors and desmoids
Turcot syndrome pairs polyposis with brain tumors
Lynch syndrome: few right-sided adenomas with mismatch repair defects
Peutz-Jeghers: hamartomatous polyps with lip pigmentation (STK11)

stem: A 16-year-old boy has had 2 days of worsening abdominal pain that has moved to the right lower quadrant, with vomiting and a temperature of 39°C (102.2°F). He has marked right lower quadrant tenderness, and the total leukocyte count is 16,000/mm³. At surgery the appendix is swollen with a purulent coating. He has no rash, asthma, recent travel or splenomegaly.
oneliner: 16M + 2 days RLQ pain, fever 39°C + WBC 16,000 + swollen appendix with purulent coating → which white-cell differential?
ask: Which differential best describes his leukocytosis?

whyNot.A: Basophilia accompanies **myeloproliferative disease**; he has **no splenomegaly** or blood disease
whyNot.B: Eosinophilia fits **allergy, asthma or parasites**; he has **none** of these and no rash
whyNot.C: Lymphocytosis fits **viral** illness; he has a **purulent** focal infection
whyNot.D: Monocytosis fits **chronic** infection or recovery; his illness is **2 days** old

answer: Neutrophilia with a left shift (bacterial infection)
why: Acute appendicitis is a **bacterial** infection of an obstructed appendix. Bacterial infection drives marrow release of **neutrophils**, including immature **band forms**, a **left shift**, so the neutrophils rise.

idea.rule: Bacterial infection raises neutrophils with a left shift; viral raises lymphocytes; parasites and allergy raise eosinophils.
also: Viral infection such as infectious mononucleosis: lymphocytosis
Parasitic infection or asthma: eosinophilia
Tuberculosis and endocarditis can give monocytosis
CML raises basophils along with granulocytes

stem: A 1-day-old boy has green (bilious) vomiting after his first feeds and mild abdominal distention. He passed meconium in the first day, was born at term after a pregnancy without polyhydramnios, and has no dysmorphic features. A plain radiograph shows gas in the distal small bowel and colon. An upper gastrointestinal contrast series is performed.
oneliner: 1-day-old boy + bilious vomiting + mild distention + passed meconium + distal bowel gas, no polyhydramnios → which contrast finding?
ask: Which imaging finding is most likely?

options.E: Dilated colon with a transition zone

whyNot.A: This is **duodenal atresia**, which leaves **no gas beyond the duodenum**; his film shows **distal bowel gas**, and there was no polyhydramnios
whyNot.B: Pyloric stenosis causes **non-bilious** projectile vomiting at **2 to 6 weeks**, not on day 1
whyNot.D: Meconium ileus gives **failure to pass meconium** in cystic fibrosis; he **passed meconium**
whyNot.E: Hirschsprung disease causes **delayed meconium passage**; he **passed it** on day 1

answer: Malrotation with volvulus: abnormal duodenojejunal junction with a corkscrew duodenum
why: Incomplete midgut rotation leaves a narrow mesenteric stalk that can twist around the **superior mesenteric artery**. The upper GI series shows the **duodenojejunal junction to the right of the midline** instead of left of the spine, and a **corkscrew duodenum**.

idea.rule: Bilious vomiting in a newborn is malrotation with volvulus until proven otherwise.
also: Volvulus can infarct the midgut, so surgery (Ladd procedure) is urgent
Double bubble means duodenal atresia
Pyloric stenosis presents with non-bilious projectile vomiting at 2 to 6 weeks
Hirschsprung disease shows a transition zone and delayed meconium passage
